segments.voice: Yesterday, the Markandeya, and a ring for the worst day: if you can't let go, keep company with the good. Today, a different Purana, a harder subject, and a look back at the week.

When someone dies, a house goes quiet in its own way, and in some Hindu families a book is read aloud over the days that follow. It's the Garuda Purana, or the part of it about what happens after death. Some people hear it with comfort. Some find it frightening, and some have only heard the frightening parts secondhand. So before the passages themselves, the frame: who is asking, and why.
screen: `A QUIET HOUSE.` → `A BOOK READ ALOUD.` → `FIRST, WHO IS ASKING?`

segments.voice: Garuda is the great eagle, the bird Vishnu rides. In this Purana, Garuda has questions, and Vishnu answers them. In one section, the one people mean when they name the book at a time of mourning, Garuda asks about death: where a person goes, and what the living can do. The next three days read those passages, with three things to carry in. It's a question asked out loud, by a devoted bird to his god. The book isn't only about death; other sections turn to worship, medicine and gems. And readers differ about how to hear it: as a description, as a moral picture, or mainly as a rite for the family. This path won't rank those readings. Now the week, before it closes. Kandu, whose one evening lasted centuries. Vyasa in the river, calling the hard age excellent. Harishchandra's promise, and Vasishtha's anger. Two betrayed men, and a refrain that keeps bowing. Madalasa at a cradle. A ring for the worst day. And now, an eagle asking about death.

segments.voice: Close your eyes, and let someone you've lost, or someone you love, come gently to mind, only as much as feels right today. Breathe with them there, slowly and kindly. If you pray, you can hold them before God.
